cardiolipin.definition: A fat molecule found almost only in the inner wall of mitochondria. It helps the parts that make energy work together.

inner-mitochondrial-membrane.definition: The folded inner wall of a mitochondrion. This is where most of the cell's energy is made.

barth-syndrome.definition: A rare inherited disease, mostly in boys and men. A faulty gene changes cardiolipin, which can weaken the heart and muscles and cause tiredness.

primary-mitochondrial-myopathy.definition: A group of inherited diseases in which faulty mitochondria make the muscles weak and tired.

six-minute-walk-test.definition: A simple test of how far a person can walk in six minutes. Trials use it to measure fitness and stamina.

left-ventricular-ejection-fraction.definition: The share of blood the main pumping chamber of the heart pushes out with each beat. A low value means the heart pumps weakly.

eosinophilia.definition: A raised number of eosinophils, a type of white blood cell that takes part in allergies and some infections. A blood count shows it.

benzyl-alcohol.definition: A preservative that stops germs growing in some multi-dose medicines. It can be dangerous for newborn babies.

cd36.definition: A protein on the surface of heart, blood-vessel and other cells. In rat hearts, hexarelin attached to it.

vasoconstriction.definition: Narrowing of a blood vessel. When the heart's own arteries narrow, less blood reaches the heart muscle.

collagen.definition: The main building protein of skin, tendons and scars. It gives tissue its strength.

dermis.definition: The skin has two main layers: the thin outer epidermis, and the thicker dermis below it, which holds collagen, blood vessels and nerves.

diabetic-foot-ulcer.definition: An open sore on the foot of someone with diabetes. It often heals slowly because nerves and blood flow are damaged.

cosmetic-product.definition: A product put on the outside of the body, such as skin, hair or lips, to clean, protect or change its look. Anything injected is not a cosmetic.

medical-device-clearance.definition: A US route that lets a medical device, such as a wound dressing, be sold when the FDA finds it similar to one already on the market. It is not a drug approval.

nad-plus.definition: A small molecule in every cell that carries energy-related chemical reactions and helps some repair enzymes. It is made from vitamin B3.

coenzyme.definition: A small helper molecule that an enzyme needs to do its job. Many coenzymes are made from vitamins.

niacin.definition: Vitamin B3. It comes in several forms, such as nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, found in food. The body uses them to make NAD+.

nicotinamide-riboside.definition: A form of vitamin B3 that cells can turn into NAD+. It is sold as a food supplement.

nicotinamide-mononucleotide.definition: A molecule one step before NAD+ in the cell. It is sold as a supplement in some countries; the rules differ from country to country.

novel-food.definition: A food or ingredient that people did not commonly eat in the past. In Great Britain it may only be sold after a safety check and an authorisation.

efsa.definition: A food-safety agency whose scientists assess foods and food ingredients and publish their safety opinions. It gives advice; it does not decide what may be sold.

dietary-supplement.definition: A product swallowed to add nutrients, such as vitamins, to the diet. In the US and the UK it is regulated as a food, not as a medicine; Canada and Australia have their own categories.

new-dietary-ingredient.definition: In the US, a supplement ingredient not sold before October 1994. The maker must tell the FDA why it is expected to be safe before selling it.

listed-medicine.definition: In Australia, a lower-risk medicine, such as a vitamin pill, made only from ingredients on an approved list. It carries an AUST L number. The TGA does not check whether it works before it is listed.

gras.definition: A US food term: 'generally recognised as safe'. A company may tell the FDA about its GRAS view; an FDA 'no questions' letter is not a medicine approval.

wada-m2.definition: The anti-doping rule that bans drips or injections of more than 100 mL in 12 hours, whatever they contain, unless given in hospital care or with an exemption.

beta-3-adrenergic-receptor.definition: A receptor on fat cells that adrenaline switches on to release stored fat.

osteocalcin.definition: A protein made by bone-building cells. Its level in blood is used as a sign of how fast bone is being renewed.
